intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that B-cell immunodeficiency, distal limb anomalies, and urogenital malformations (BILU), also known as Hoffman syndrome, is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TOP2B gene (126431) on chromosome 3p24.

checks.claim: BILU syndrome (Hoffman syndrome) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TOP2B gene.

paragraphs.text: BILU syndrome, also called Hoffman syndrome, is an autosomal dominant syndromic B-cell immunodeficiency. Broderick et al. (2019) described it as agammaglobulinemia or hypogammaglobulinemia with facial dysmorphism and limb anomalies. Other reported features include urogenital malformations, and patients have absent or reduced B cells with normal T cells (Edery et al., 2001; Papapietro et al., 2020).

paragraphs.text: Hügle et al. (2011) concluded that their mother-daughter pair and the sporadic girl reported by Hoffman et al. (2001) had the same condition, which they called Hoffman syndrome. The acronym BILU (B-cell immunodeficiency, limb anomalies, and urogenital malformations) was used for the autosomal dominant disorder described in 2 unrelated families (Tischkowitz et al., 2004; Papapietro et al., 2020). Papapietro et al. (2020) concluded that BILU syndrome and Hoffman syndrome are the same disease, TOP2B deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Hoffman et al. (2001) reported a 6-year-old girl with isolated humoral immunodeficiency and an unusual combination of dysmorphic features. She had microcephaly, micrognathia, sickle-shaped eyebrows, hypoplastic alae nasi, thenar hypoplasia, triphalangeal thumbs, partial syndactyly of toes 4 and 5, recessed great toes, hypoplastic first metatarsals, an anterior anus, and hypoplastic labia minora. She also had postnatal growth retardation and developmental delay, and her development was substantially slower than that of her twin. She had recurrent sinopulmonary infections and pneumococcal bacteremia. Laboratory evaluation showed hypogammaglobulinemia, absent B cells, and a 46,XX karyotype. Searches of the literature and the London Dysmorphology Database found no matching syndrome, and the authors suggested that she might represent a new syndrome of unknown cause.

paragraphs.text: Broderick et al. (2019) studied 2 unrelated families with autosomal dominant syndromic B-cell immunodeficiency. Ages at presentation were 7 and 35 years in family 1 and 6 years in family 2. The probands had recurrent infections with polysaccharide-encapsulated bacteria, severe hypogammaglobulinemia, absent CD19+ B cells, facial dysmorphism, and limb anomalies. T-cell responses to mitogens were normal. The patients formed no germinal centers and did not develop protective serologic titers after immunization. However, detectable circulating immunoglobulins indicated that some B cells were present below clinical limits of detection. CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell numbers were normal, and NK cells were reduced in 2 patients. A third patient (family 3), who presented at 5 years of age, was first reported as having an atypical form of ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome and was later found to have humoral immunodeficiency with no detectable peripheral B cells and normal T-cell mitogen stimulation. No malignancy had been observed in these patients.

paragraphs.text: Edery et al. (2001) suggested that the association of B-cell immunodeficiency, distal limb abnormalities, and urogenital malformations in a 3-generation family might be a new autosomal dominant syndrome. Tischkowitz et al. (2004) reported a second family with autosomal dominant inheritance and suggested that the association was a true syndrome. Hügle et al. (2011) described an affected mother and daughter. Papapietro et al. (2020) showed that the TOP2B mutation in family A arose de novo in an affected woman and was passed to her affected daughter, and Broderick et al. (2019) identified a de novo heterozygous TOP2B mutation in 1 of their families. Both findings are consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Broderick et al. (2019) performed whole-genome sequencing of affected and unaffected members of 2 families with Hoffman syndrome. TOP2B was the only gene with a heterozygous variant in each family that was present only in affected members. One variant was a de novo in-frame deletion (c.1761_1763delAGA; p.EE587E) and the other was a missense mutation (c.1448C-T; S483L). The authors did not state which variant occurred in which family. In a third patient, independent reanalysis of clinical whole-exome sequencing found a heterozygous c.1897G-A transition in TOP2B, resulting in a gly633-to-ser (G633S) substitution. All mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and all 3 affect the TOPRIM (DNA gating) domain. The authors noted that TOP2B has a probability of loss-of-function intolerance (pLI) of 1, which suggested disease through haploinsufficiency or partial dominance. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, constructs carrying the patient mutations failed to complement a temperature-sensitive top2 allele and did not support recovery of top2-null haploid spore clones, indicating loss of topoisomerase II function. Strains heterozygous for the mutations grew more slowly and decatenated kinetoplast DNA less effectively than wildtype, indicating a partial dominant-negative effect.

paragraphs.text: In the Cypriot BILU family (family A), Papapietro et al. (2020) identified a heterozygous c.1453G-C transversion in TOP2B, resulting in an ala485-to-pro (A485P) substitution. It was the only coding mutation absent from the healthy parents (I:3 and I:4). It arose de novo in their affected daughter (II:4) and was passed to her affected daughter (III:1). Sanger sequencing found the same mutation in the patients of the French family (family B). Recombinant TOP2B A485P had more than 10-fold lower DNA relaxation and decatenation activity. Coexpression with wildtype TOP2B lowered decatenation activity, which suggested a dominant-negative effect rather than haploinsufficiency. TOP2B protein was reduced in patient T cells, fibroblasts, and iPSCs. In HEK-293 cells, the mutant protein produced a degradation product, suggesting reduced stability, but it still interacted with TOP2A.

paragraphs.text: Broderick et al. (2019) found that Top2b mRNA and protein were more highly expressed in wildtype mouse B cells than in T cells. They proposed that the disorder is restricted to B cells because loss of topoisomerase function preferentially reduces transcription of long genes. They noted that mouse B-cell transcription factor genes (EBF 390 kb, Pax5 178 kb, Foxo1 85 kb) are much longer than T-cell genes (Tcf1 30 kb, Notch1 45 kb) or shared genes (Rag1 11 kb, E2A 24 kb). In published ChIP-seq data and etoposide-induced END-seq breaks from mouse primary B cells, Top2b, but not Top2a, was found at the promoter and the intron 5 enhancer of Pax5. This suggested that defective Top2b activity could impair germline transcription and Igh locus accessibility, with negative effects on V(D)J recombination.

paragraphs.text: Broderick et al. (2019) also made knockin mice carrying the mouse equivalent of the patient EE587E mutation. Homozygotes were not viable. Top2b +/EE587E heterozygotes had a reduced spleen-to-body ratio, reduced total serum IgG, impaired antigen-specific antibody responses to ovalbumin and Pneumovax-23, and fewer B cells at most developmental stages. Their B cells showed reduced Pax5 and Foxo1 expression and increased DNA strand breaks. Peripheral B cells were reduced even compared with Top2b +/- mice, whereas T cells were unaffected. After LPS stimulation, with or without IL-4, heterozygous B cells secreted less total IgG, IgG3, and IgG2b, and more than 90% did not advance beyond the first division. Splenic T cells produced normal amounts of IL-2 in response to PMA and ionomycin and proliferated normally, consistent with the normal T-cell mitogen responses seen in patients. No malignancy was observed in the mice.
